title: UNH Launches International Space Partnership with Space Hub Yorkshire - University of New Hampshire
content: UNH’s long expertise in space science extends to the edge of our solar system and beyond —and now, across the Atlantic to the United Kingdom. From left: Jennifer Miksis-Olds, UNH interim vice president for research and innovation, West Yorkshire mayor Tracy Brabin, and Space Hub Yorkshire founder Glann McCauley from the University of Leeds at the signing of the partnership agreement between UNH and Space Hub Yorkshire. Last month, UNH signed a partnership agreement with Space Hub Yorkshire to strengthen collaboration in space research, innovation, and skills development. The agreement, called a concord, establishes a framework for developing joint initiatives to benefit academia and industry and will help to forge stronger links between their respective geographies to drive investment and export opportunities between them. “UNH has a deep and growing connection to space and aerospace research and industry here in New Hampshire and New England,” says Jennifer Miksis-Olds, UNH vice president for research and innovation, who signed the agreement. “I look forward to extending opportunities for our students, researchers, and industry partners with Space Hub Yorkshire.” The formal signing ceremony took place July 23, 2026, during the Farnborough International Airshow in the U.K., a leading aerospace industry event that UNH attended, along with New Hampshire’s Department of Business and Economic Affairs and the New Hampshire Aerospace and Defence Coalition. But the relationship between UNH and Space Hub Yorkshire (SHY) began several years ago during a trade mission visit from the mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, to Concord, New Hampshire. “This new partnership reflects our ambitions to ensure that businesses, universities and students across West Yorkshire have access to the skills, opportunities and support they need to thrive,” Brabin says. “International collaboration is essential to advancing innovation, strengthening our economy, and preparing the workforce for the opportunities of tomorrow,” says State of New Hampshire Department of Business and Economic Affairs Commissioner Lucy Lange. “The partnership between UNH and Space Hub Yorkshire reflects an important commitment by the business community and higher education to prepare the workforce for high-demand careers and create lasting connections that strengthen the investment, entrepreneurship, and talent pipeline driving economic growth.” Representatives from SHY will come to Durham this fall for the Northeast Space, Technology, Trade, and Research (STTAR) Expo at UNH. The Oct. 28–29 event, presented by UNH, N.H. Business and Economic Affairs, and the N.H. Aerospace and Defense Coalition, is the region’s premier aerospace gathering, bringing together brings together industry leaders, researchers, government agencies, manufacturers, startups, investors, educators, and workforce partners to explore the technologies shaping the future of space and aerospace innovation. title: Can northern forests continue to be an effective carbon sink? - University of New Hampshire
content: Researchers record measurements high above the canopy in Bartlett Experimental Forest. (Photo courtesy of Northern Arizona University) Forests have played a vital role in a changing world by removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in trees and soil. But a new study conducted in the Bartlett Experimental Forest, located just west of Conway, New Hampshire, found that its ability to absorb more CO₂ than it releases has declined over the last 20 years. Moving forward, just how much we can rely on these forests to help slow the accumulation of carbon in the atmosphere? The research team, led by Andrew Richardson, a professor at Northern Arizona University and former postdoctoral associate at UNH, and Darby Bergl, a doctoral student at NAU, and including New Hampshire Agricultural Experiment Station scientist Scott Ollinger, professor of natural resources and the environment at UNH, took advantage of an exceptionally rare 20-year record of measurements taken at Bartlett to ask a simple question: Are temperate forests continuing to absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere as expected? They found that the answer — at least at this site — was, increasingly, no. Their findings were published in Global Change Biology Communications. Between 2004 and 2023, the research team found that the carbon sink strength of Bartlett, a mature forest that has been extensively studied since its establishment by the USDA Forest Service in 1931, declined substantially. The decline was not caused by a reduction in photosynthesis or wood growth, as the researchers had expected. Instead, it was driven by increasing carbon release from the ecosystem through respiration, the natural process by which plants, roots, and soil microbes emit carbon dioxide. “Over that time period, there’s been a steep decline in the amount of carbon dioxide the forest sequesters annually, and a primary cause seems to be warming winter temperatures,” says Ollinger, who is also on the faculty of the Earth Systems Research Center. “Long-term observations like these are critical for understanding whether forests can continue to provide one of nature's most important defenses against rising atmospheric carbon dioxide.” In several recent years, the forest even became a net source of carbon rather than a sink. "We often think of forests as one of our best natural climate solutions because they remove large amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, so changes in their ability to store carbon could have important consequences,” says Bergl. “Our findings suggest that mature temperate deciduous forests may no longer reliably remove more carbon than they release under continued global change.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: GOP, Dem State Senators Call for Audit of the University System of New Hampshire - indepthnh.org
content:
InDepthNH.org (https://indepthnh.org/2026/08/12/gop-dem-state-senators-call-for-audit-of-the-university-system-of-new-hampshire/) CONCORD — A bipartisan group of state Senators have called for a fiscal and performance audit of the University System of New Hampshire (USNH), alleging a lack of transparency, accountability, and that it is not investing enough money in instructing students. In the official letter to Chairman Gerald Griffin dated July 31, 2026, the Joint Legislative Performance Audit and Oversight Committee requested that “the Legislative Budget and Audit Division conduct a performance audit of the University System of New Hampshire.” It was signed by Senate President Sharon M. Carson, R-Londonderry, Sen. Timothy Lang, R-Sanbornton, Sen. Donovan Fenton, D-Keene, and Sen. Suzanne M. Prentiss, D-West Lebanon. Neither Carson, Fenton, or Prentiss could be reached for comment Wednesday. A statement from the USNH said in response: “The University System of NH (USNH) operates with transparency regarding its operations and expenditures. The system’s annual financial audits are posted online, meetings of the board of trustees are public, and members of the legislature serve on the board. We look forward to understanding more about the nature of the request and supporting the timely work of the audit committee.” Sen. Timothy Lang, R-Sanbornton said, “As we saw recently, the University System of New Hampshire has called for the merging of the president’s position at UNH with the chancellor’s position. There were many of us in the legislature that did not feel that was appropriate… We wanted to have a much better understanding of what that looks like, what’s going on, and how that performance is working.” Lang continued that he’s not sure merging the two positions is good for all Granite Staters, noting concern that the merger could minimize the influence of KSC and PSU. “I just think this is in the best interest for all the citizens of New Hampshire, to have that performance audit so we understand how the University System works better,” Lang said. The USNH Board of Trustees voted on June 26 to approve consolidating the two positions — which would mean the presidents of KSC and PSU would report to the new position — though the two institutions would retain their independence. Lawmakers will decide whether to approve it during the next legislative cycle. In the press release from the New Hampshire Senate, Senate President Sharon M. Carson, R-Londonderry said that this isn’t about politics; it’s getting the facts first. “Before making sweeping changes, we need a comprehensive review to understand where we are and what the implications could be—not only for faculty and staff, but most importantly, for our students and the communities these learning institutions call home,” Carson said. She could not be reached for further comment. In the official letter to Chairman Gerald Griffin dated July 31, 2026, the Joint Legislative Performance Audit and Oversight Committee requested that “the Legislative Budget and Audit Division conduct a performance audit of the University System of New Hampshire.” It was signed by Senate President Carson, Sen. Lang, Sen. Fenton, and Sen. Prentiss. The letter reads: “To ensure the system operates efficiently and effectively an external financial statement audit is statutorily required on an annual basis. It is important, however, for the Legislature in its policy- making role to be informed of improvements that can be made to the System’s administrative operations. “The performance audit should include, but not be limited to, a review of the organizational staffing structure of the System and the proposed merger between the Chancellor’s Office and the Office of the President of the University of New Hampshire.” Chancellor of USNH Catherine Provencher could not be reached for comment. Data released by the House Republican Majority Office breaks down the expense category for USNH and their percentages of its total operating expenditures. It also noted that “about 25 cents of every operating dollar goes to direct instruction. Central administration, fundraising, academic support, and student services together total roughly $196 million, nearly as much as instruction itself ($230 million).” It also clarified that UNH is the bulk of the system: $717M of the $925M in operating expenses (77%). The data also noted that instruction costs are $229.9M, which is about 25% of the $924.7M in total operating expenses. It explained that state general appropriations fall from $95M (FY25) to $87M (FY26) and $77M (FY27), and that “USNH says it will restructure academic and administrative activities to align costs with lower revenue.” It also highlighted how self-insured medical and dental claims and fees jumped from $77M to $94.2M in one year, adding it was a main factor in rising compensation costs. In a press release from the House Republican Majority Office, Deputy House Majority Leader Joe Sweeney, R-Salem said: “We entrust our University System with tens of millions of taxpayer dollars, it is only right that we expect efficient and wise investments in return. Accountability does not happen behind closed doors. It is time to open up the books, shine a bright light on every single corner of our university system, and show where every dollar is going. The people demand this transparency. “Every dollar not spent on classroom instruction is a dollar not invested in the future of the Granite State, and those dollars need to be scrutinized and analyzed now more than ever. I look forward to this audit taking place timely so when the next State Budget is crafted next year, we will have the insight we need to shape the future that Granite Staters deserve.” Public Works Director Nate Hadaway and Fire Chief Michael Weden are pictured at the podium at Wednesday night's planning board meeting in Lincoln. title: Bit by Grit - University of New Hampshire
content: If you were building a team to design a light switch for someone with disability, you’d probably include an electrical engineer. Is that all, though? You might also need someone who could understand the user’s specific needs, a mechanical engineer to design the moving parts, an industrial engineer to choose materials, and someone who could keep the team working efficiently. “There are so many different roles,” says Claes Thelemarck, UNH Extension 4-H educator, as he spoke to a group of more than 100 teen participants in the inaugural Grit to Grow Summit held in June in Meredith, New Hampshire. The summit, designed by UNH Extension 4-H and the UNH Extension Grit to Grow Collaborative, gave teenagers a chance to meet face-to-face with people who represent a wide range of industries and who would love to welcome such young collaborators and problem solvers into their field. As an exercise to kick off the summit’s second day, Thelemarck challenged small groups of attendees to think of a reason why a person might have trouble using a conventional light switch and then build one that the person could operate. One group made a switch that could be operated by foot. Another group designed a button that could be pressed by any body part. Yet another group used braille to designate the switch’s positions. Each group found their own path to a solution, and each group member found a way to lend their unique talents. The light switch problem is small in comparison to the challenge facing each of the teenagers attending the summit. They all need to figure out how to navigate the end of their high school years and the beginning of whatever comes next. The Grit to Grow Summit was designed to help them chart such a course. Organizers designed the event to address an information and access gap that many young people deal with. They are thinking about their post-high school plans but don’t have enough practical knowledge to build a plan, particularly if they don’t want to immediately enroll into post-secondary school. The first day of the summit featured several workshops, ranging from identity to decision-making and personal finance, and the second day cycled participants through the Church Landing Conference Center in Meredith, where they could pepper prospective employers with questions. Alex Cousino, a student at Kearsarge High School in North Sutton, developed a strong interest in robotics through his local 4-H club. This summer, he’s been restoring a ’72 Chevelle. So, Cousino was all ears when he approached the display for Draxle, a company that offers remote auto repairs and services. “They were talking about how I could earn money by fixing other people’s cars,” Cousino says, “and that would go wonderfully with what I’m hoping to do, which is own a garage.” A junior from Manchester, Katalina Hoxaj plans on following in her father’s footsteps as a property developer. She found plenty at the summit to lend definition to her vision of her future. Hoxaj gained valuable insight from people working in agriculture, banking, and others, noting that she was very glad to have "in-depth, one-on-one conversations with people working in these industries” during the summit. “And I also got offered a job internship, running social media for the NH Timberland Owners Association,” she reports. While the event was designed to serve young people, the employers and educational institutions who participated all reported value in the summit. Rudy Glocker, founder of the apparel company Burgeon Outdoors in Lincoln, New Hampshire, was one of the many employers who came with the hopes of connecting with the next generation of employees. He says that he wanted to tell attendees about the opportunities in their home state. “We want to raise awareness that we are offering a skilled job here in the White Mountains,” Glocker says. Burgeon makes its clothing at either its Lincoln or Gorham locations and is willing to hire “novices” and develop their skills. “There’s a high demand for our products and we need more people making them.” The interactivity of the event, in which groups of attendees worked with employers to discuss the challenge of plotting a career path in 2026, was one of the most valuable to Becky Marden, a nurse and career coach who works as the director for workforce development at Elliot Hospital. “For me, it’s all about hearing from the students themselves,” says Marden. “During these interactive sessions, they ask great questions, and their answers will actually drive some of the work that we do.” Marden — like other employers at the summit — observes that the landscape looks different to today’s teenagers than it did for the generation currently in management positions. And it continues to change, Marden adds, emphasizing the need to “Never stop asking…We have to know what (the students) want and what they’re looking for.” The adults weren’t the only ones doing the asking, according to Doug Cullen, workforce development manager for the New Hampshire Timberland Owners Association. He says that he attended the event to make sure that attendees knew that forestry, and the wide range of careers found within, was an option for them. “They’re definitely engaging,” Cullen says about the youth in attendance. “What they’re looking for is an opportunity to find people that can actually have conversations with them.” Organizers of the summit say they were looking to create an experience in which the next generation of workers could engage with employers, and that it succeeded to the benefit of both groups. “The event exceeded our expectations,” says Shana Brunye, chief operating officer for Bring Back the Trades, a strong partner who leveraged her network of trades professionals to support the event. She says that industry presenters came away inspired by the young people, particularly by their social intelligence. “The students were encouraging their peers, helping them to think about options for the future, and advocating for trades pathways.” The interactions with young people brought several of their concerns to the surface, says Daryl Luter, president of the construction management firm Fulcrum Associates. “I do feel that we collected enough potential program data with the questions and the conversations we all had together during the breakout sessions,” Luter says, “that we should be able to better tailor some of the speaking sessions next year.” Kate Korbas, the Extension program leader who provides administrative oversight to UNH 4-H efforts and the person who conceived the idea for the summit, says the success of the event is owed to the many who helped turn the concept into reality. “It was an outstanding demonstration of a true partnership initiative, bringing together partners from the Community College System of NH, NH Career and Technical Education, and of course, industry,” Korbas says. “The greatest comment I heard from a teen was that the experience helped them feel good about not knowing exactly what was next for them but that there were multiple paths they could take with a great deal of support from education, community, and industry leaders.” That comment echoes Thelemarck’s remarks at the conclusion of his light switch challenge, when he noted that some might know what kind of career they want but many don’t. “What I do know is that you are all problem solvers,” he announced to the crowd “You’ve shown that to everyone here, that you can collaborate and you can problem solve. And no matter what field you choose to go into, that’s something you can take to the bank.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: A River at Risk - University of New Hampshire
content: The Wind River Indian Reservation in Wyoming is vast — spanning 2.2 million acres, it is one-third the size of New Hampshire. It contains river canyons and glaciers, mountains and plains, and a complex political, natural, and environmental history. In partnership with the Wind River tribes, Teresa Cohn and Iva Moss-Redman in the UNH College of Life Sciences and Agriculture are working with Wind River communities to assess damaged river systems to determine what might be remediated. The Wind River is the lifeblood of the reservation, connecting headwaters to canyons, providing water to communities, and supporting the wild lands and wildlife for which the area is known. Initially dammed about 100 years ago, the river and its adjacent ecosystem have undergone significant changes that have affected life in the area, but they have been difficult to quantify and analyze in the years since. Moving forward, a healthy river system is essential to the continuation of indigenous life ways. “We’re looking at the needs that the Wind River tribes have,” says Moss-Redman, a research scientist in Cohn’s lab and a member of the Northern Arapaho tribe who also teaches on the reservation. “Once we clearly identify those needs, the team at UNH will be able to respond to them.” Cohn, an associate professor in the UNH department of natural resources and the environment, leads a long-term collaborative research project investigating changes along the banks and on the land near the Wind River, known as the riparian zone. In the arid climate — the area averages less than 10 inches of rain per year — the riverside vegetation and animal life play vital roles in the local environment. Cottonwood species are foundational in this environment, stabilizing banks, regulating water temperatures, and providing food and nesting habitats for wildlife, but they are in decline. Characterizing and quantifying these and other riparian changes provides important insights for how they impact the tribes and the cultures that developed in concert with now-shifting natural conditions. Historically, data from aerial photographic surveys provided low-resolution comparisons of vegetation abundance at different time points but lacked species-specificity. Assisted by UNH colleague Ben Fraser’s GIS/GPS expertise, the team carried out a baseline vegetation characterization last year. “We’ve had a lot of back-and-forth with the tribes over the past year and a half, looking at what’s going on with their riparian food webs,” says Cohn. “That way we can better understand what changes are most significant.” Moss-Redman has a doctorate in Indigenous Knowledge Systems and incorporates the studies being done on the reservation into her science curriculum in Wind River Reservation schools. Research to assess wildlife along the river, with nearly 200,000 trail camera photos documenting the variety of animal life in the area over the last few years, has provided students with a compelling topic. The students learn about indigenous research methods, develop their own research questions and plans, and analyze data generated by the research being done. “Indigenous research methods are helping the students access their knowledge systems from either the Arapaho or Shoshone tribe to help them understand how relationships, respect, reciprocity, and responsibility are applied during a research project,” says Moss-Redman. Nell Davis, a graduate student and teaching assistant in the department of natural resources and the environment, is another member of the team studying the river system. She is looking at the geological foundation of the floodplain and cottonwood ecosystem and how that can affect future management strategies. “I’m talking with people in the area and working to connect our findings with their lives,” says Davis. “This includes thinking about how our results could be integrated into land-based lessons that teach students about connections between wildlife, geologic features, and the changing river.” Other changes are coming to the river system that will require additional responses and adaptation. The large glaciers in the Wind River Mountain Range are retreating and will provide less meltwater to the river system over time. And more volatile weather patterns are yielding highly variable snowpack depths year to year in the mountains, potentially further reducing the meltwater supply during many spring thaws. “In an arid climate, less meltwater can have a profound effect on the riparian environment,” says Cohn. The Wind River system is also being affected in another way. An outside mining firm processed uranium on the reservation in the 1950s and early 1960s, producing a substantial amount of uranium supply for the United States during the Cold War era. The operation was shut down in 1963, but the site was not remediated at the time, with 1.8 million cubic yards of dangerous material, known as tailings, left in the open for more than 20 years. Contamination has since been found in the groundwater, making many wells toxic, and is now beginning to enter the river water as well. While investigations have detected contamination in crayfish, the Tribes are interested in better understanding how the uranium may be moving through riparian food webs. “The Wind River tribes have a strong interest in maintaining indigenous ways of working with the land and ways of life in general,” says Cohn. “Part of that is learning about the conditions they have now, including the contamination, and working to track and monitor them. The team at UNH is fortunate to be able to contribute to these efforts.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: UNH awarded $8 million to launch statewide initiative to study ticks, diseases, the environment - East Boston Times-Free Press
content:
Summertime in New England can mean getting outdoors to hike, garden, and head to the beach, but that can all come with a challenge — avoiding tick bites and tick-borne diseases like Lyme disease. Thanks to an $8 million grant from the National  Science Foundation (NSF), a new initiative led by the University of New Hampshire could help provide more insight. The project is bringing together scientists from across the Granite State to launch an ambitious statewide research and education initiative focused on one of the region’s fastest-growing  public health concerns: ticks and the diseases they carry and their impact on people, wildlife, outdoor recreation, and the environment. Colleges & Universities The initiative, known as EMBEDDEd-NH (Endeavor for Multi-Omics-Based Exploration, Data-Driven Modeling, and Education in New Hampshire), comes at a critical time since New Hampshire consistently ranks among the states with the highest incidence of Lyme disease in the nation — often ranking in the top ten. “Ticks are an issue that touches nearly every community in New Hampshire,” said Dr. David Needle, clinical professor of molecular, cellular and biomedical Sciences and senior veterinary pathologist of the New Hampshire Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at UNH.  “By combining cutting-edge science with statewide collaboration and education, we have an opportunity to build knowledge that benefits both our state and the broader scientific community.” Parasites & Parasitic Diseases Needle is leading the four-year initiative that includes experts in the fields of genomics, ecology, and artificial intelligence, as well as an opportunity for undergraduate involvement, to better understand tick-borne disease risks. Researchers plan to investigate how ticks survive, spread, and transmit disease by using advanced genomic sequencing, microbiome analysis, environmental monitoring, ecological modeling, and machine learning. They will examine how climate, habitat, wildlife hosts, and microbial communities influence tick biology and pathogen transmission across New Hampshire’s diverse ecosystems. Health Conditions The project will focus on three important tick species found in New Hampshire: • The blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis), the primary vector of Lyme disease, • The winter tick (Dermacentor albipictus), which has major impacts on moose and wildlife health. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, emergency room visits have been higher than normal in many parts of the U.S. and in April, the rate of ER visits for tick bites was the highest for that time of year since 2017. Health officials and researchers are increasingly concerned not only about established tick-borne diseases, but also about the emergence of new pathogens and the spread of additional tick species into the region. Ecology & Environment Tick populations and tick-borne illnesses, including Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, Powassan virus, and other emerging infections, continue to expand across the Northeast. Recent research shows that ticks are also showing up more in cities along the East Coast, not just in wooded areas. Warmer winters, changing land use, shifting wildlife populations, and expanding human development have all contributed to rising tick encounters and disease risk. “Ticks are more than just disease vectors,” Needle said. “They have wide roles as parasites, prey, and hosts of diverse microbes. Their varied lifecycles, wide and increasing dispersal, and status linking ecosystems and ecological scales make ticks a powerful system for studying how genomes, microbes, hosts, and environments interact in a rapidly changing world.” Science The researchers, students, and community partners come from the University of New Hampshire, Keene State College, Plymouth State University, state agencies, and industry collaborators to study the ecology and evolution of ticks across New Hampshire. The initiative also places a major emphasis on education and workforce development. Undergraduate students across the state will participate directly in research through course-based research experiences, summer research programs, internships, and fellowships. Students will gain hands-on experience in genomics, bioinformatics, artificial intelligence,  ecology, and data science — fields that are increasingly important to the state’s scientific and technology workforce. Along with potential scientific discoveries, EMBEDDEd-NH hopes to inspire more students to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and public health. Educational Resources The project builds on existing investments in New Hampshire’s research infrastructure, including UNH’s Hubbard Center for Genome Studies, statewide data  science resources, and collaborations with public health and environmental agencies. Researchers say the work of the new EMBEDDEd-NH initiative could ultimately help improve disease surveillance, inform public health responses, support wildlife management, and guide future environmental decision-making. Health UNH also offers tick testing to the public through UNH Extension. The service can detect the presence of a pathogen in a tick in as little as three days. For more information go to unh.how/tick. EMBEDDed-NH is supported by funding from the National  Science Foundation’s EPSCoR E-RISE program, which supports statewide research infrastructure, workforce development, and collaborative scientific innovation in emerging research areas. Colleges & Universities The University of New Hampshire inspires innovation and transforms lives in our state, nation and world. More than 15,000 students from 50 states and 87 countries engage with an award-winning faculty in top-ranked programs in business, engineering, law, health and human services, liberal arts and the sciences across more than 200 programs of study.  A Carnegie Classification R1, land, sea and space grant institution, UNH has FY25 research expenditures of more than $188 million, to further explore and define the frontiers of our world. title: New UNH athletic director Colton committed to community, generating revenue for department - UnionLeader.com
content:
Clear skies. Low 59F. Winds light and variable.. Both the baseball and softball teams at Southern New Hampshi… Ty Miles played in each of the University of New Hampshire’s… Ryan Colton is introduced on Tuesday at UNH’s new director of athletics. DURHAM — Ryan Colton wanted to learn what makes University of New Hampshire athletics special, so he turned to some of the school’s legendary former head coaches. Colton, who was named UNH’s new athletic director on July 27 and introduced to the university on Tuesday at Wildcat Stadium, said he has recently spoken with former Wildcats men’s hockey coach Dick Umile, football coach Sean McDonnell and field hockey coach Robin Balducci. They each told him the people at UNH are what makes it a special place. “I’m looking forward to meeting all the people who are not just in athletics but really across this campus that support us and want the university and Wildcat athletics to be successful,” Colton said. “That was really the key pieces of advice that I got from them.” UNH men’s hockey coach Mike Souza said the fact Colton reached out to some of the school’s past coaching greats meant a lot to both them and the current coaches. During his introductory press conference, Colton said his decisions will be made with the student athletes in mind first and foremost and that he wants to build up and harness the UNH athletics community. “I think he’s a humble guy that seems very smart and one that understands that — he mentioned it in his comments — that it’s about the student athletes first, it’s about the people,” said Souza, UNH’s ninth-year coach and former Wildcat player. “It’s what’s made us run here for a long time. I think he has a grasp of that.” Colton, who grew up in Taunton, Mass., succeeds Allison Rich, who was UNH’s athletic director from 2022 through the 2025-26 school year. Colton spent the past eight years at the University of Richmond as its deputy athletic director and chief of staff. He was the athletic director’s chief adviser and worked in areas of the department like business operations, Name Image and Likeness (NIL) initiatives, human resources and legal affairs. Before transitioning to college athletics, Colton was a lawyer and involved in politics. The Bucknell University graduate — he was a quarterback for the Bison football team — previously worked at Providence College and the College of the Holy Cross. “I think one of the things that (Richmond athletic director) John Hardt taught me was you don’t build these things overnight,” Colton said. “I’m really excited to get started and get to work but it really is going to take long, sustained hard work to build out the athletic department that I think we can have here.” Colton was at Richmond for the football program’s final seven seasons in the Coastal Athletic Association (CAA), of which UNH is a member, before the Spiders went to the Patriot League last year. Richmond is among several schools that have left the CAA in recent years. First-year UNH football coach and former Wildcats quarterback Sean Goldrich said he wants to work with Colton on how the program can maximize its ability to be successful regardless of changes that happen within the CAA or at the FCS level. Goldrich called the football program a blue-collar operation. Players want to continue the Wildcats’ winning tradition, Goldrich said, and he wants to work with Colton on how best to sell the university to potential recruits. “It doesn’t really take all the bright lights ... for us to get back to where we’ve got to go, but you’ve got to get the right people in the door,” Goldrich said. “We’ll continue to talk about how we’ve got to do that.” In his research and conversations with people, Colton said he has learned that the men’s hockey team’s success is critically important to UNH athletics. Giving the men’s and women’s hockey programs the resources to compete within their conference, Hockey East, is high on Colton’s to-do list, he said. When the UNH men’s hockey team is humming, Souza said it helps the university’s 19 other athletic programs. Souza and UNH women’s hockey coach Hilary Witt are entering the final season of their current contracts. “Most athletic departments have an engine,” said Colton, who received a UNH hockey jersey from university president Elizabeth S. Chilton during Tuesday’s introduction. “We’re looking forward to diving in and finding ways that we can support them and making sure they’re successful.” Colton on Tuesday stressed the importance of generating revenue for the department. While it will be efficient and responsible with its current resources, the department must be creative, innovative, and aggressive in growing new revenue, he said. Revenue generation has always been an important issue in college athletics but never more so than now, Colton said. Colton wants to get under the hood of the department and identify where UNH’s opportunities are to bring in more money. “We’re in three really competitive conferences (CAA, Hockey East, America East), so we’re going to need more resources to compete at the highest levels,” Colton said. title: Is UnitedHealth’s Margin Going Back To What It Was? - Trefis
content: UnitedHealth’s operating margin has dropped well below its own long-run level, and by the company’s own account the repair in its commercial business is a multi-year job rather than a finished one. UnitedHealth (UNH) has returned about 67% over the last twelve months, and it now trades about 6% below its 52-week high. Anyone who has held through that run is carrying one question: has the profit margin come back the way the share price has? On the company’s own reported numbers the margin has not, and its own account of the commercial repair explains why. Four Cents Of Operating Profit Where There Used To Be Eight Measured through the June 2026 quarter, UnitedHealth’s operating margin is 4.2% against a 14-year company history of 8.0%, with gross margin at 18.8% against 24.2%; taken across its metrics, the combination sits further from that record than any prior reading. The medical care ratio did improve, to 86.7% in the June quarter from 89.4% a year earlier, though $860 million of net favorable prior period medical development, the majority of it in-year, helped it there. That is the shape of the recovery so far: real, assisted, and a long way from the old margin. Whether a business keeps earning what it used to earn is the whole test of a compounder, and on that test this one is not there yet. In its commercial benefits business, medical cost trend is running modestly above 11%, and management names the mechanisms: arbitration under the No Surprises Act, where the average award to an out-of-network provider is now 11 times what Medicare would pay, and heavier provider coding of office visits and emergency department care. Neither is a quick fix, and the sticky trend has pushed full commercial margin recovery past 2027. Medicare is the part that works: the margin on that product line, not the company-wide one, is guided to finish 2026 above 3%. Medical cost trend there is running below plan, helped by benefit design, network curation and a lighter respiratory season, even as Medicare Advantage enrollment declines. The squeeze is not only medical: the operating cost ratio moved the wrong way, 12.7% in the June quarter against 12.3% a year earlier, as technology and AI spending went in. Margins that hold up are one of the things the Trefis High Quality Portfolio insists on in its holdings. Management has put guidance behind the improvement. UnitedHealth has guided full-year 2026 adjusted earnings to a range of $19.50 to $20 a share and raised the outlook for Optum Health, the arm that delivers primary and specialist care, ambulatory surgery and home health, to at least $2.2 billion of full-year operating earnings. What the guidance does not do is put the old margin back, and that is the gap between a share price that has recovered and a business that has not. A holder deciding whether to add here can see how the whole picture scores on the five-factor scorecard. The number to watch is the medical care ratio: the company guides 88.1% for full-year 2026, plus or minus 25 basis points, against 86.7% in the June quarter, and a finish above that range would say the reset is the level rather than the dip. title: Ty Miles is UNH's lineman of many skills - UnionLeader.com
content:
Clear skies. Low 59F. Winds light and variable.. UNH’s Ty Miles holds the line during the Wildcats’ 2025 opener at North Carolina Central. Ty Miles played in each of the University of New Hampshire’s 13 games last season, and if he looked out of place it was for good reason. Miles, who graduated from Londonderry High School, lined up as an interior offensive lineman in practice last year, but was used exclusively as a tight end on game day. “I started a couple games, but it was at tight end mostly blocking,” Miles explained Monday during the team’s annual media day. “Nothing technically on the O line. None of those guard, center or tackle spots. I was playing tight end the whole time. “I would play center, guard and tackle in practice, but then when it was game time I would end up playing tight end. I had a couple routes. They never threw it to me though.” Versatility is one of Miles’s strengths. He’s been playing primarily guard and tackle on the right side of the line this summer as the Wildcats prepare to open their CAA season at Albany on Friday, Aug. 28. He said he has no preference between guard and tackle. “Athletically, I feel like I’ve always been great outside playing tackle, but I can still move inside and get guard reps,’ he said. “Either way I feel great at both positions. “Still kind of determining where I’m going to be going into the season. Still trying to earn that spot. That’s where I’m sitting at right now.” Miles, a 6-foot-5, 315-pound junior (academically), wore No. 91 early in his UNH career, but will wear No. 72 this year. He was No. 75 when he played at Londonderry. “The good thing about Ty is he’s versatile,” UNH head coach Sean Goldrich said. “You can move him around a bunch of different positions. At this point in camp we’re moving the final pieces to make sure we find the best five that fit, but he’s going to play somewhere for us at a high level. “He’s been awesome to work with. He’s another blue collar, tough, gritty kid who just shows up and works every day. He has a lot of good football in front of him.” As a freshman, Miles didn’t get any game action until the final four games of the regular season. That was by design so he could preserve his redshirt season. He was allowed to play in UNH’s FCS playoff game against UT Martin without burning his redshirt. “I was still a little bit behind physically back then, I felt,” Miles said. His playing time increased last season, but the UNH coaching staff clearly felt he was most valuable when the team lined up in multiple tight end sets. That staff is gone, as former head coach Rick Santos left UNH to become the head coach at Penn during the offseason. Goldrich hired all new assistants when he was hired to replace Santos. Miles said his decision to remain at UNH following the coaching change was a good one. “We showed up here for spring with a new staff and it was great,” he said. “We had a team meeting, kind of setting that standard that nothing was going to change. The goals were still the same, just different people running it. “This new coaching staff is young, but they keep the energy high. The staff is great. Though many investors started 2026 assuming that the Federal Reserve would eventually lower interest rates, another trajectory has emerged amid Middle East conflict and renewed inflation concerns: not only has the Fed appeared comfortable keeping interest rates elevated until inflation can be tamped down, but some analysts have even predicted that rate increases could be in store. The Fed kept its benchmark rate in a target range of 3.5% to 3.75% at its July 29 meeting, while three voting members preferred a quarter-point rate increase. Fortunately, some companies have consistent cash flow, strong balance sheets and limited dependence on inexpensive financing. Those traits can matter more when rates remain steady or even increase. That shifts the focus away from companies waiting for borrowing costs to ease and toward companies that can keep compounding without lower-rate help. Businesses tied to transaction volume, recurring revenue or essential demand are better positioned than those whose growth depends on cheaper financing. This transaction fee model has allowed Visa to generate consistent revenue and earnings growth even if the broader economic environment shifts. With the secular shift toward cashless payments worldwide and the growing trend of rising cross-border payment volumes, Visa is a prime beneficiary. A look at Visa's latest earnings report helps to confirm. For Q3 2026, the company reported strong net revenue growth of 14% year over year (YOY) alongside earnings per share (EPS) growth of 11% over the same period; both topped analyst predictions. This growth was due to impressive payments volume and processed transactions growth of 10% each. What's more, the company has seen a mixture of commercial payments volume improvement, Visa Direct transaction growth, and value-added services revenue increases; it is not relying on a single part of its business to fuel gains. Visa's excellent financial profile, including robust free cash flow, allows it to pay out a stable dividend while also making aggressive share repurchases and ongoing investments into new technologies to support its growing payments network. This could be why the company has 31 Buy ratings and not a single Sell or Hold, signaling unanimous analyst support. In the company's Q2 2026 earnings report, Spotify highlighted improvements, including 14% YOY revenue growth, a 21% YOY increase in gross profit, and gross margins that rose to 33.4% from 31.5% a year prior. Free cash flow has also climbed, increasing by 14% YOY to 797 million euros (approx. $920 million). A combination of improving profitability and subscriber growth (total monthly active users climbed by 12% YOY) led to these results. What helps Spotify to thrive despite higher interest rates is the combination of its margin, income, and free cash flow gains alongside its Premium subscriber growth, a sign that customers have generally accepted the company's price increases. Subscription-based models like Spotify's generate predictable recurring revenue, and the company's advertising arm helps offer an additional pathway for longer-term growth as well. An impressive 20 out of 26 analysts have rated SPOT shares a Buy, and the company has nearly 25% upside potential. As healthcare utilization tends to remain mostly stable throughout economic cycles, a company like UNH can generate steady revenue regardless of interest rate activity. This is not to discount the impact of reimbursement trends, regulatory changes, and other factors, though these elements are often manageable for a company of UNH's size and scope. This is perhaps why UNH was recently able to raise its full-year 2026 outlook for adjusted EPS and operating earnings even as commercial medical costs remain elevated, and Medicaid remains highly pressured. Tesla, notably, is mentioned 87 times in SpaceX's latest S-1 filing. Musk is the largest shareholder of both companies, fueling speculation that his automotive, AI and space ventures could eventually merge. Tesla owns about 19 million SpaceX shares, while the companies already collaborate on AI tools, chip development, and computing infrastructure. Kalshi traders currently predict a 50% chance of a Tesla-SpaceX merger before May 2027, while Polymarket places the odds at 43% before the end of 2026. Wolfe Research said that the potential for an eventual SpaceX-Tesla merger has "increasingly moved into the mainstream," with some investors now making it their primary reason for owning Tesla stock, Investing noted. Wolfe said that the merger thesis rests on three pillars: Musk's growing voting control, the potential to create an AI powerhouse combining Tesla's real-world data with SpaceX's computing infrastructure, and access to a larger capital base. Morningstar sees a similar logic, saying that Tesla and SpaceX are becoming increasingly intertwined through AI initiatives, chip development and supply-chain ties. SpaceX has bought over $500 million worth of Tesla Megapacks and $130 million worth of Cybertrucks. Morningstar said that Tesla's robotaxi platform could eventually leverage Grok and Starlink, adding that the "most important additional reason" for a merger is Musk's desire to bring his businesses under "one conglomerate," enabling talent, tech and resources to move more freely across companies. While SpaceX is expected to debut at a valuation above Tesla's $1.5 trillion, Morningstar believes Tesla shareholders may have more leverage than investors assume. The firm said that Tesla investors may be reluctant to accept a deal that values Tesla below SpaceX, especially given SpaceX's soaring valuation and negative free cash flow. "Ultimately, we think Tesla shareholders may agree to a deal that gives Tesla at least 50% of the combined company, but they may want even more control," Morningstar said. The research firm estimated a "66%-34% Tesla/SpaceX equity ratio" based on its fair-value assumptions. Morningstar also said it "wouldn't be surprised to see a deal occur within a year of the SpaceX IPO." Despite the growing enthusiasm, both firms see major obstacles. Wolfe said that a merger would likely require a substantial premium, could face opposition from existing SpaceX shareholders, and may attract regulatory scrutiny due to Tesla's extensive operations in China. Wolfe ultimately believes a deal remains "unlikely until mid-2027 (at the earliest)." Morningstar also raised similar concerns, noting that SpaceX is a major U.S. government and military contractor, while Tesla maintains significant manufacturing and battery operations in China. content: U.S. stock futures were subdued early Wednesday as traders digested President Donald Trump’s State of the Union address and geared up for the earnings report from AI bellwether Nvidia later in the day. As of 3:00 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nasdaq and Russell 2000 futures gained 0.1%, while S&P 500 and Dow futures were flat with a positive bias. Meanwhile, retail sentiment toward the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 Index, has moved to ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’ a day ago, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ETF, which tracks the Nasdaq 100 Index, has remained ‘bearish’ amid high message volumes. Nvidia (NVDA): Beyond its earnings, focus also remains on export controls. U.S. officials have reportedly confirmed that, despite recent approvals, Nvidia has not yet sold any flagship H200 chips to China. Watch for any spillover impact on competitors' shares, such as AMD and Intel, as well as on key vendor TSMC.Netflix (NFLX), Warner Bros Discovery (WBD) & Paramount (PSKY): The merger drama is heating up, with WBD saying that Paramount’s revised $31 bid is ‘potentially superior’ to the existing Netflix deal. Paramount’s new offer also includes $7 billion regulatory breakup fee. UnitedHealth (UNH), Oscar Health (OSCR) and others: Trump said during his State of the Union (SOTU) speech that he wants to end Affordable Care Act premium tax credits and redirect funds directly to consumers, rather than large insurance companies. TeraWulf (WULF): The crypto miner gained ahead of its earnings print today. Also, Trump, in his SOTU speech, announced the Rate Payer Protection Pledge, under which tech companies have said they will ensure that their massive AI buildouts do not drive up consumers' electricity bills. (LCID): The company confirmed a 12% reduction in its U.S. workforce after revising its 2025 production figures. In addition, we successfully executed multiple high-yield bond offerings to finance two of our existing HPC projects at Barber Lake and Black Pearl,” said Tyler Page, Chief Executive Officer. The therapy is to treat adults and children with Friedreich’s ataxia (FA), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder causing nervous system damage. The FDA’s decision follows encouraging clinical data from Larimar’s ongoing open-label study and a recent Support for Clinical Trials Advancing Rare Disease Therapeutics (START) pilot program meeting. The agency also agreed that skin FXN could serve as a novel surrogate endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, supporting the planned Biologics License Application (BLA) submission targeted for June 2026. The Trump administration is reportedly looking to deploy a Pentagon-built artificial intelligence system to help establish benchmark prices for critical minerals. Officials will initially apply the U.S. Department of War’s Open Price Exploration for National Security (OPEN) AI pricing model to four critical minerals: germanium, gallium, antimony, and tungsten, according to a Reuters report on Tuesday. The OPEN program focuses on metals that are traded in very low volumes. Next year, it will move under the control of the non-profit Critical Minerals Forum (CMF). CMF said it works with government-funded partners to test AI pricing models and support commercially viable mining and processing projects. This comes days after a Bloomberg report stated that the U.S. was moving forward with a price-floor system for critical minerals to reinforce supply chains tied to national security. The plan, crafted by several federal agencies, is being reviewed with allies as Washington looks to shield Western companies from pricing pressure linked to Chinese supply dominance. Trump, who has been very vocal about strengthening the country’s critical minerals supply chain, recently announced that his administration plans to establish a strategic stockpile of critical minerals, supported by $10 billion in initial funding from the U.S. Export-Import Bank. Earlier this month, U.S. Vice President JD Vance introduced a proposal to form a preferred trade bloc among allied nations focused on critical minerals. The plan includes coordinated price floors to reduce China’s influence over materials essential to semiconductors, electric vehicles, and advanced defense systems. China has long dominated the processing of several key minerals and has used that position to influence global supply and pricing. U.S. officials say the new strategy is designed to stabilize markets and help allies diversify supply sources. Critical minerals companies traded higher at the time of writing, with MP Materials (MP) up 3%, Critical Metals (CRML) rising 2%, and USA Rare Earth (USAR) jumping more than 5%. It also requires the expiration of four business days to match Paramount’s offer, the termination of WBD’s merger agreement with Netflix, and then entering into a definitive merger agreement with Paramount.
